A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reward-machine learning work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including appendices A–B in v2 and A–E in v3.

before.justification: v2 reports original GridWorld, BlockWorld, and robotic-arm experiments, plus analysis of mice trajectories. Results include recovered reward machines, solver statistics, and demonstration-size analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds held-out mice evaluation, recovery from arbitrary stochastic policies, node-bound sensitivity, and transfer experiments.

M1.justification: The main SAT/MAX-SAT learning procedure is retained. For the new sensitivity and transfer experiments, Algorithm 4 adds an auxiliary product-policy construction that accumulates prefix-conditioned probabilities, normalizes them, and fills unsupported rows uniformly; v2 specifies direct assignment in Equation 10.

E1.justification: The original domains remain. Appendix C adds a two-node BlockWorld task driven by arbitrary stochastic policies, and Appendix E adds transfer to a GridWorld with rearranged rooms. The held-out mice experiment uses the existing population and dataset.

E2.justification: v2 provides a uniform-policy reference for mice policy distance in Appendix B.3. v3 adds dense-feature D-IRL and label-feature F-IRL comparisons in the held-out mice experiment, node-bound experiment, and transfer experiment (Table 4, Table 7, Figure 12). Uniform policies also participate in the new mice and transfer comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 adds a 180/20 training/test split for mice with average trajectory log-likelihood, node-bound evaluation using 10,000 length-100 rollouts per model, and transfer evaluation on 100 expert trajectories. The retained stack experiment changes prefix depth from 9 to 10. The 100-trajectory stack-avoid setting is removed from the appendix table.

E4.justification: New Appendices C–E test recovery without policy optimality, sensitivity to an underspecified node bound, and transfer across room rearrangements. These substantially extend the existing non-stuttering, false-positive robustness, and demonstration-size analyses.

E5.justification: The confidence-bound construction and alpha-based filtering in Section 4.1 are retained. Neither version reports seeds, repeated independent fitting runs, performance uncertainty intervals, or significance tests. The new trajectory and rollout counts describe evaluation sample sizes.

E6.justification: v3 adds held-out mice results: LRM −9.81, D-IRL −28.99, F-IRL −28.57, and uniform −30.49 average log-likelihood (Table 4), plus new Appendix C–E outcomes. Retained results also change: patrol with non-stuttering goes from 7,264 negatives and 0.81 seconds to 3,076 and 0.51 seconds; the 5,000-demonstration stack result changes from four to eight solutions. Stack results at depth 10 replace depth-9 results, preventing a same-setting performance comparison.

T1.justification: The definitions, propositions, sufficient-depth bound |S|umax², and Appendix A proof arguments are retained. Appendix A.1 explicitly marks the learned, extended transition function where v2 used abbreviated notation; this does not introduce a different argument or guarantee.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's central contribution statement, and conclusion retain the same claims about policy-equivalent recovery from finite-depth prefix-tree policies and extension to demonstrations through MAX-SAT. The non-optimal-policy experiment supports a property already stated in v2 Remark 2.

C2.justification: New Section 6 explicitly discusses exact-label assumptions, vulnerability to perceptual noise, and potentially exponential clause growth despite the polynomial depth bound. Appendices D–E add interpretations of approximate task preservation, graceful degradation with fewer nodes, and transfer performance approaching the ground-truth model.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the promised post-acceptance code release with a specific stated public-repository link. It also specifies equal unit MAX-SAT weights, baseline feature representations, and auxiliary policy-construction details. Existing PPO training, discretization, hardware, and mice preprocessing disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds Cook (1971) for SAT complexity, Parac et al. (2024) for learning from noisy labels, and Ziebart (2010) for maximum causal entropy IRL. The principal related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain unchanged; other reference edits are bibliographic corrections.

P1.justification: v3 adds brief SAT background, corrects wording and Reacher terminology, converts Section 3.1's numbered subsections to run-in headings, and inserts a limitations section and Appendices C–E. Most existing exposition and its ordering are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial new visual evidence through Tables 4 and 7 and Figures 10–12, including reward-machine diagrams and a transfer grid/bar-chart comparison, plus Algorithm 4. Existing Figures 1–9 remain, while Table 3 and Algorithms 2–3 are relocated and appendix displays are reflowed.

improvement.justification: The held-out mice comparisons and node-bound/transfer tests strengthen empirical validation, while explicit noise and scalability limitations make applicability easier to assess. However, revised appendix tables introduce inconsistencies absent in v2: Appendix B.1 still claims four solutions for 5,000 stack and 1,000 stack-avoid demonstrations, whereas v3 Tables 5–6 report eight. The added evidence improves the paper, but these reporting discrepancies limit the gain.
